cover.headline: A 40%-margin visa franchise at under 10x earnings: cheap, but volumes have stalled, growth now comes at thin margins and the sector has de-rated by 40%
cover.lead: BLS International runs visa centres for 46 governments (Spain, Italy, Germany via iDATA, India's missions) and a listed digital arm (BLS E-Services, ~53%). Q1FY27 revenue rose 25% and EBITDA 24%, but visa applications were flat and EPS rose only 11% as tax, depreciation and minorities took more. We forecast EPS of ₹18.1 / ₹21.1 / ₹24.1 for FY27-29E. The street (IDBI Capital, the only active broker: Buy, ₹330) values BLS on **P/E**. On the house rule we start from its own one-year-forward P/E median since Apr-2021 (18.6x) and apply the sector move of the travel + internet set used for TBO Tek (IRCTC, Thomas Cook, Info Edge, IndiaMART vs five-year medians, −40%). **11x Sep-28E EPS of ₹22.6 = {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): we initiate with HOLD.** The result sits just below the BUY line and the peer set matters: with IRCTC's five-name set the value is ₹300, with no sector move ₹420; the DCF (Ke 12.5%) says ₹513. Bull {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.h: The visa business is excellent, but its margin gain is over
arguments.p: Visa & Consular earns ~90% of group EBITDA at a 40.1% margin (14.6% in FY22) after BLS took its centres in-house and sold more value-added services. Management now guides "maintain ~40%" and says net revenue per application is "stabilising". Applications were flat at 11.3 lakh in Q1FY27; growth is price, mix and contract wins.

arguments.h: New growth earns a fraction of the visa margin
arguments.p: Aadhaar Seva Kendras (₹2,055 cr UIDAI order) add ~₹400 cr a year of revenue by FY28E at 10-15%; Digital (39% of revenue) earns ~8% and ~47% of it belongs to outside shareholders; Atyati (₹157 cr, Jul-2026) adds ₹275 cr of revenue at 7.5%. So revenue grows {{F.salesGrowth.0|pct0}} in FY27E but EPS only {{F.epsGrowth.0|pct0}}.

arguments.h: Government and tender risk is real, as 2025 showed
arguments.p: The MEA barred BLS from new Indian-mission tenders for two years on 9-Oct-2025 (complaints including charging for optional services); the Delhi High Court quashed the order on 18-Dec-2025 on process, leaving the MEA free to issue a fresh, specific notice. Contracts are re-tendered every 3-10 years and country revenue is not disclosed.

arguments.h: Valuation: cheap against its history and its cash, less so against its peers
arguments.p: At ₹218 BLS trades at 10.3x FY28E and 9.7x Sep-28E EPS vs a 18.6x forward median since 2021; net cash is ₹1,617 cr (~₹39 a share). But its travel and internet peers trade 40% below their own medians, and foreign funds cut their stake from 10.9% to 4.1% in eighteen months. We need visa volumes or a contract win to be more positive.

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): visa applications after the West Asia war, Atyati's first quarter, the Aadhaar ramp and D&A.
New global tenders (management cites a US$1-2 bn pipeline over the next one to two years) and renewals of existing European contracts.
Any fresh MEA show-cause notice, or new Indian-government awards now that the debarment is quashed.
Capital allocation: further acquisitions (~₹2,000 cr budget over four to five years) or a buyback (not under consideration as of Aug-2026).
UAE corporate-tax changes affecting the free-zone subsidiary (management: ~1 point on the group rate).

sections.title: A visa-centre operator that earns 90% of its profit from 61% of its revenue, plus a fast-growing, thin-margin digital arm

blocks.p: BLS International runs visa application centres for foreign governments. An embassy outsources the front office (appointments, document checks, fingerprints and photos, passport return) and keeps the decision; the applicant pays BLS a service fee on top of the visa fee and can buy extras (premium lounge, courier, SMS, form filling, insurance). The government pays nothing, so BLS earns on volume, the fee set in the tender and how many extras it sells. It works for 46 governments in 100+ countries: Spain (global contract since 2016), Italy, Portugal, Poland, Slovakia, Cyprus and Canada among them, Germany and Italy through iDATA (Turkey, bought in FY25) and the Indian government itself (passport, visa and attestation services at Indian missions abroad, and from FY26 visa centres in China and Aadhaar Seva Kendras in India). It also sells residency and citizenship-by-investment advice (Citizenship Invest, Dubai) and owns a UK hotel. Its listed subsidiary **BLS E-Services** (BLS 51% at Mar-26, 53% after Apr-Aug 2026 purchases) is a different business: banking-correspondent outlets for SBI and other banks, assisted e-government services, loan distribution (Aadifidelis, 57%) and, from Jul-2026, Atyati Technologies.

blocks.callout: **Why the MEA episode matters even though it was overturned.** The court set the order aside on process, not on the merits of the complaints. The MEA kept the right to issue a fresh, specific notice on service quality. India is BLS's home market and one of its largest clients (Indian missions, China centres, attestation, now Aadhaar), and the case showed that a client government can try to shut BLS out of future tenders. We treat it as a live risk in the bear case and in the governance score, not as a closed chapter.

sections.title: A duopoly-like niche that is still growing, as more governments outsource and more people travel

blocks.p: Global visa market ~US$7.7 bn by value (2024; outsourced ~US$2.2 bn ex-USA, 31%) and ~133 mn applications (outsourced ~38%); outsourced value seen growing ~14% a year to ~US$3.2 bn by 2029 and the outsourced share of applications from 38% to 50% (industry estimates in the company deck). Consular outsourcing ~US$134 mn (2024); investment migration ~US$0.9 bn. Two global leaders: VFS Global (unlisted; Blackstone/Temasek-owned) and BLS, followed by TLScontact (Teleperformance), iDATA (now BLS), Visametric (now BLS) and regional players. Governments award 3-10-year, usually exclusive, country or regional contracts by tender; the applicant pays (user-pay), so the price is set in the tender and value-added services carry the margin.

bullets: **Growth comes from three places:** more cross-border travel (outbound from India, the Gulf, China and Africa); more governments outsourcing (the outsourced share of applications ~38% in 2024, seen at ~50% by 2029); and more spend per applicant (value-added services, premium lounges, home biometrics).

**Against it:** Outbound travel from India, the Gulf, China and Africa to Europe/North America; digital/e-visas and visa-free arrangements reduce in-person applications over time (the company itself lists the shift to digital visa applications as an industry trend).

**How contracts are won:** by tender, typically for 3-10 years and exclusive by country or region. Technical scores (security, biometrics, data protection, track record) decide eligibility; price decides the winner. Incumbents usually renew, but losses happen and bidders litigate (the MEA order cited BLS's own tender challenges).

blocks.callout: **So what:** the industry tailwind is real but modest (high single digits in volume, low teens in value, on the company's own industry figures), and it is a tender market: growth arrives in lumps when contracts are won and can disappear when one is lost.

sections.title: Visa & Consular: a 40% margin business whose volumes have stopped growing; Aadhaar adds revenue at a third of the margin

blocks.p: The segment earned ₹738 cr of EBITDA on ₹1,840 cr of revenue in FY26 (40.1%), ~90% of group EBITDA. Revenue grew 11% in FY26 and 22% in Q1FY27, but the Q1 growth was not from visas: applications were flat at 11.3 lakh (West Asia war; new Slovakia and Cyprus volumes offset losses elsewhere). Net revenue per application rose 11% to ₹3,521 on newer, better-priced contracts and more value-added services; Citizenship Invest earned ₹17.5 cr (₹11 cr), the UK hotel ₹16 cr (₹2.5 cr) and the new Aadhaar centres ₹17.5 cr. Excluding Aadhaar and the hotel, segment revenue grew ~15%. Management says net revenue per application is now "stabilising" because almost all centres are already self-managed, and guides 10-15% growth for the business.

blocks.h: The Aadhaar Seva Kendras: big revenue, small margin

blocks.p: UIDAI awarded BLS a ₹2,055 cr work order to set up and run Aadhaar Seva Kendras (enrolment and update centres) across India for six years, paid per transaction like a visa centre; Bihar added a ₹100 cr enrolment project. Capex is ~₹125 cr in three phases (₹75 cr spent by Aug-2026), which is why D&A rose 39% in Q1FY27. Management expects ~₹2,500 cr of revenue over six years, full run-rate from Q4FY27-Q1FY28, at a 10-15% EBITDA margin (it said 15-20% in May). We model ₹180 / 400 / 420 cr for FY27-29E at 12.5%: by FY28E Aadhaar is ~15% of segment revenue but ~5% of its EBITDA, and it pulls the segment margin from 40% to ~36%.

sections.title: Digital Services: 39% of revenue, ~10% of EBITDA, and ~47% owned by outside shareholders

blocks.p: BLS E-Services (listed; BLS ~53%) runs ~1.58 lakh banking-correspondent and citizen-service touchpoints: cash deposits and withdrawals for SBI and other banks (GTV ₹29,500 cr in Q1FY27, +13%), assisted e-government services, insurance and, through Aadifidelis (57%, bought Nov-2024), loan distribution, where BLS earns 2-2.5% of each loan and passes most of it to agents (4-5% EBITDA margin). Aadifidelis contributed ~₹225 cr of the ₹330 cr Q1FY27 segment revenue. Revenue more than doubled in FY26 (₹1,158 cr) and grew 32% in Q1FY27, but the margin is 7.0% (8.0% in Q1). Atyati Technologies (bought 2-Jul-2026 for ₹156.82 cr; ~₹275 cr revenue, ₹20-21 cr EBITDA) adds a BC network for non-SBI banks and banking software from Q2FY27.

In FY28E we expect it to earn ~₹154 cr of EBITDA, of which outside shareholders own roughly half. The segment matters more as a source of cash-hungry acquisitions (Aadifidelis, Atyati) than as a profit engine.

sections.title: A narrow moat: scale and track record in a two-player niche, but every contract is re-tendered

verdicts: One of two global scale players: 46 client governments, 100+ countries, 44.1 lakh applications in FY26; the iDATA and Visametric purchases removed a mid-sized rival in Germany/Italy-facing markets.
Wins eligibility in technical scoring; does not decide price.

Contracts are exclusive for 3-10 years but are re-tendered: incumbency helps (infrastructure, security clearance, track record) but does not guarantee renewal. Governments can and do switch (e.g. the MEA's debarment attempt in 2025).
Visibility for 3-10 years, then a re-tender.

Fees are set in the tender and paid by applicants; value-added services and self-managed centres lifted net revenue per application from ₹1,613 (FY23) to ₹3,302 (FY26), but management says it is now 'stabilising'.
Further gains depend on value-added services, which regulators and governments watch (the MEA order cited them).
Spain and Indian government work are large (Indian missions ~12% of revenue in Q1FY26); country revenue is not disclosed
One lost tender can take a visible slice of profit.
BC banking, assisted services and loan distribution are open, low-margin markets (4-8% EBITDA margins)

blocks.callout: **Verdict:** A real but narrow moat: scale, compliance track record and a duopoly-like market structure in government visa outsourcing, against re-tender risk, client concentration (Spain and Indian missions), political risk and low switching costs at renewal. Digital Services has no moat (BC and loan distribution earn 4-8% margins).

sections.title: Revenue 6x and owners' profit 14x since Covid; the margin jump is done and growth is slowing

blocks.p: BLS earned ₹786 cr of revenue in FY20 and ₹478 cr in Covid-hit FY21, when visa centres shut. Since then revenue has grown to ₹2,998 cr (FY26) and owners' profit from ₹50 cr to ₹687 cr. Two different engines did this. From FY22 to FY25 the visa business took its centres in-house (from a partner-run to a self-managed model) and sold more value-added services, so the Visa & Consular EBITDA margin rose from 14.6% to 34.5% (40.1% in FY26) on revenue that grew ~15% a year (FY23-25). From FY25 acquisitions took over: iDATA and Citizenship Invest in visa, Aadifidelis (loan distribution) in digital, which more than doubled Digital revenue in FY26 at a 7% margin. So consolidated revenue grew 37% in FY26 but EBITDA 30% and owners' EPS 35%; in Q1FY27 revenue rose 25% and EPS 11%.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** the easy margin gain is behind BLS. Visa margins are at ~40% and management only promises to hold them; volumes were flat in Q1FY27; the new growth (Aadhaar centres at 10-15%, loan distribution at 4-5%, BC banking at ~8%) earns a fraction of the visa margin. Each rupee of new revenue therefore adds less profit than the average, and the tax-plus-minorities leakage is rising. Revenue can grow 20%+ while EPS grows in the low to mid teens.

sections.title: Little capital needed, ~₹2,500 cr of cash generated in five years, much of it spent on acquisitions

blocks.p: Visa centres are leased and applicants pay up front, so BLS needs little capital: cash capex was ₹137 cr in FY26 (₹161 cr in FY25) against ₹903 cr of operating cash flow. Over FY22-26 it generated ~₹2,530 cr from operations. About ₹1,010 cr went into acquisitions (₹82 cr net in FY23 for Zero Mass, 88% bought in Jun-2022 at a ₹120 cr valuation; ₹899 cr in FY25: iDATA, Citizenship Invest for ₹260 cr, 57% of Aadifidelis), ~₹510 cr into capex and only ~₹220 cr into dividends; the rest built the cash pile. In FY27 so far BLS E-Services has paid ₹157 cr for Atyati Technologies and BLS ₹45 cr for more BLS E-Services shares, and the ₹125 cr Aadhaar build-out is three-quarters done. Returns are high (ROE 31-35% in FY24-26) but falling as goodwill (₹1,213 cr, half of net worth) and cash build up.

blocks.callout: **The capital question:** management wants to spend ~₹2,000 cr on acquisitions over four to five years and says each deal must earn 17-20%; when asked on the Aug-2026 call what value past deals have created, the CFO could not answer. A buyback is "not under consideration". Our forecasts assume no new acquisitions, so cash builds to ~₹{{F.treasury.2|num}} cr (net of leases and minorities at book) by FY29E: either it is spent on deals we cannot model, or it is a source of upside through buybacks.

sections.title: Earnings quality: strong cash conversion, but low tax, rising minorities and acquisition goodwill

bullets: **Cash conversion is strong.** Cash from operations was ₹903 cr in FY26, 131% of owners' profit (163% in FY25); fees are collected in advance and receivables are 21 days.

**Other income is mostly interest.** FY26 other income of ₹95.2 cr: deposits ₹52.1 cr, bonds ₹3.8 cr, debt-fund gains ₹13.6 cr, FX gain ₹7.9 cr (one-off), insurance/commission and misc. ₹17.3 cr. We build FY27E as 10% on the engine's opening net treasury of ₹729 cr (net of leases and minorities at book; ~5.8% on gross cash and deposits) = ₹73 cr, plus ₹18 cr of other items: ₹{{F.otherIncome.0|num}} cr, vs ₹95.2 cr in FY26 and ₹22.7 cr × 4 in Q1FY27.

**Tax is low and may rise.** The effective rate was 9.2% in FY26 (14.4% in Q1FY27): much of the visa profit is booked in a UAE free-zone subsidiary. Management guides ~12% for FY27; a UAE rate change or more profit in India (Aadhaar) would lift it.

**Minorities take a growing share.** Owners' profit was 95% of reported profit in FY26 (₹687 cr of ₹724 cr) and 94% in Q1FY27; outside shareholders own ~47% of BLS E-Services and 43% of Aadifidelis, the fastest-growing parts.
**Goodwill is half of net worth** (₹1,213 cr), tested annually with no impairment so far. The auditor's opinion is unmodified, with an emphasis of matter on a dormant Punjab e-governance subsidiary.
**Value-added services are the profit lever and a regulatory target:** the MEA order of Oct-2025 cited complaints about charging for optional services (the order was quashed on process).

blocks.callout: **Accounting flag: AMBER.** Cash conversion is excellent and the audit opinion clean, but three things make reported EPS less solid than it looks: a tax rate that depends on the UAE structure, a growing minority share, and a balance sheet built increasingly on acquisition goodwill whose returns management could not quantify.

sections.title: Net cash ₹1,434 cr (₹1,617 cr at Jun-26), negative working capital, and ₹1,213 cr of goodwill

blocks.p: At Mar-2026 BLS held ₹494 cr of cash, ₹688 cr of bank deposits, ₹152 cr of longer deposits and ~₹331 cr of debt funds and bonds, against ₹230 cr of borrowings (₹205 cr drawn in FY25, the year of the iDATA purchase) and ₹200 cr of lease liabilities: net cash ₹1,434 cr on the company's definition (before leases), ₹1,617 cr at Jun-2026. Part of it belongs to BLS E-Services (₹155 cr of unspent IPO money at Mar-26, most of it since used for Atyati), whose minorities own ~47%. Working capital is negative (fees are collected before the service is delivered; receivables 21 days). The big non-cash asset is goodwill and intangibles from acquisitions, ₹1,213 cr plus ₹55 cr of other intangibles, tested for impairment every year (none so far).

sections.title: Ownership: the Aggarwal family 70.4%, foreign funds down to 4.1%

blocks.p: The Aggarwal family and its investment companies own 70.39% (Jun-2026). Aggarwal family: individuals (Diwakar 5.76%, Gaurav 4.83%, Madhukar 4.80%, Vinod 4.80%, Sushil 2.43%, Alka 1.94%, Shikhar 1.92%) and family investment companies (Azadpur Finvest 4.92%, GRB, Hawai Capital, Hillman Properties, Intime Finance ~4.86% each, BLS Finvest and Goodwork Finvest 4.48% each), Mar-26. Foreign investors own 4.14%, domestic institutions 3.1%, other bodies corporate 3.05% and individuals and others 19.32% (free float ~29.6%). Life Insurance Corporation of India, Sixteenth Street Capital, Government Pension Fund Global (Norway), Dovetail India Fund, iShares Core Emerging Markets, Axis Max Life Insurance, Vanguard, Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (top shareholders named in the Q1FY27 deck; stakes not disclosed there). FIIs fell from 10.93% (Dec-2024) to 6.14% (Mar-2026) and 4.14% (Jun-2026); shareholders rose from 1.70 lakh to 2.24 lakh; promoters steady at ~70.4%..

pair.title: Foreign funds have more than halved since Dec-2024
Promoters steady at ~70.4%

blocks.callout: **Our read:** a tightly held, family-controlled company with a small free float (~₹3,000 cr at Jun-26 prices) and falling foreign ownership. Retail holders (2.24 lakh) have absorbed the foreign selling. The promoter stake fell from 74.4% (Mar-23) to 70.4% (Sep-24) while the share capital stayed at ~₹41 cr, so the family sold roughly 4% in that period; it has been steady since.

sections.title: Governance: a family-run company with related-party rent, a large pay rise for the chairman, and a government client that tried to bar it

blocks.p: Promoter-led board: Chairman (executive) Diwakar Aggarwal, Joint MD Shikhar Aggarwal (a relative of a director, per the AR), MD Nikhil Gupta, non-executive director Karan Aggarwal; independent directors include Sarthak Behuria (former Chairman of Indian Oil Corporation, per the AR), Atul Seksaria, R.P. Sinha, Dr Savita (from 16-May-2026) and Manoj Joshi (additional director from 7-Aug-2026).

verdicts: Unmodified opinion on FY26 consolidated accounts; emphasis of matter on the Punjab e-governance subsidiary; goodwill ₹1,213 cr with no impairment.
No red flags; goodwill is the judgement area.
Rent paid to the chairman ₹8.41 cr in FY26 (₹4.49 cr in FY25) and smaller rents to other family members.
Small against profit, but rising and family-linked.
Chairman became executive (Aug-2025): pay ₹4.56 cr vs ₹0.22 cr; managerial pay +18.3% vs +1.4% for the median employee; chairman at 109x the median employee.
MEA debarment (Oct-2025) quashed by the Delhi High Court (Dec-2025); the MEA may issue a fresh, specific notice on service quality.
Reputation with India's government is an open question.
~₹1,010 cr of acquisitions in FY23-26 plus ₹157 cr (Atyati) and ₹45 cr (BLS E-Services shares) in FY27; payout 15%; no buyback.
Returns on acquisitions asserted (17-20%), not shown.
Quarterly decks with segment, application and NRPA data; no country split; tax and minority details only in the annual report.
Better than most mid-caps; client concentration opaque.

sections.title: The street: one active broker (IDBI Capital, Buy, ₹330), whose target has fallen from ₹445 in six months

blocks.p: BLS is thinly covered. The only broker with a current target on 30-Sep-2026 is IDBI Capital: Buy, ₹330 (21-May-2026, after the Q4FY26 results), +51% vs the 30-Sep-2026 close of ₹218. IDBI initiated on 3-Dec-2025 at ₹445 (21.5x FY27E EPS of ₹20.7) and cut to ₹389 in Feb-2026 and ₹330 in May; its later multiple and earnings year are behind a login. Edelweiss's last note (₹604, Nov-2024) is long stale. The bulls point to quasi-annuity government contracts, a 40% visa margin, the Aadhaar order and net cash; the share price says the market does not believe the growth: the stock has fallen 34% in a year and trades at 12.7x trailing earnings.

exhibit.title: Critiques we take seriously
head: Argument
rows: Earnings quality: the jump in Visa margins (15% in FY22 to 40% in FY26) came from taking partner-run centres in-house and from value-added services; the MEA's 2025 order cited complaints about charging for optional services. Regulators could cap VAS.
Volumes stalled: 11.3 lakh applications in Q1FY27 vs 11.4 lakh a year earlier; growth now depends on price/mix, Aadhaar and acquisitions.
Acquisition-led: ₹899 cr spent in FY25 and ₹157 cr on Atyati in FY26-27; goodwill ₹1,213 cr (49% of net worth) and management could not quantify value created when asked (Aug-2026 call).
Minorities: ~47% of the fast-growing digital arm belongs to outside shareholders.
Low tax (~9-12%) rests on the UAE free-zone structure; a UAE tax change or a shift of profit to India raises it.
Related-party rent (₹8.4 cr to the chairman in FY26) and a sharp rise in the executive chairman's pay (₹0.22 cr to ₹4.56 cr).

sections.title: Our honest summary: a 40%-margin visa franchise at 9.7x Sep-28E EPS; HOLD, because the sector and the stock have de-rated for reasons that are not all wrong

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** one of two global visa-outsourcing leaders (46 client governments, 44 lakh applications a year, ~40% segment margin), a six-year Aadhaar contract, a fast-growing but thin-margin digital arm (~47% owned by others), ₹1,617 cr of net cash (Jun-26) and ROE near 30%.

**What you are paying:** 12.1x our FY27E and 9.7x Sep-28E EPS for ~13% a year EPS growth, flat visa volumes, re-tender and government risk, a low tax rate that may rise, and a management that prefers acquisitions to buybacks. Since 2021 the market has paid a median 18.6x forward. On the house rule (own median × the travel + internet sector move of −40%) the target is {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): HOLD. With no sector move it would be ~₹420; with IRCTC's five-name set ~₹300; the DCF says ~₹513.

**This is close to the BUY line, and the peer set decides it.** The house rule takes BLS's own forward P/E median (18.6x) and applies the four-name travel + internet move (−40%): 11x. With IRCTC's five-name set (−26%) the value would be ~₹300; with no sector move ~₹420. We do not pick the friendlier set (§7c).
**We would turn buyers below ~₹220** and sellers above ~₹260 on today's numbers; sooner either way on a large contract win or loss.
**Biggest swing factors:** the multiple (each 1x is ~₹23 a share), visa volumes, and the tax-plus-minority rate (17.5% in FY27E; each point is ~1.2% of EPS).

head: Term
What it means
rows: A government hires a company to run its visa application centres (VACs): appointments, document checks, biometrics, passport return. The embassy still decides.
The applicant, not the government, pays the outsourcer's service fee (set in the tender).
Optional paid extras: premium lounge, courier, SMS updates, form filling, photocopies, insurance, home biometrics.
Visa revenue less cost of services (partner and vendor shares), divided by applications: what BLS keeps per applicant.
Centres run by a local partner who takes a share of the fee, vs centres BLS runs itself.
A UIDAI centre where residents enrol for or update their Aadhaar (India's biometric ID); BLS is paid per transaction.
An agent outlet that offers basic banking (deposits, withdrawals, account opening) on behalf of a bank; paid a commission per transaction. GTV = gross transaction value.
Programmes that grant residency or citizenship in return for an investment; Citizenship Invest advises applicants.
The Ministry of External Affairs; under Rule 151 of the General Financial Rules a ministry can bar a supplier from its tenders.
Outside shareholders of subsidiaries; their share of profit is not BLS shareholders' profit.

Half of FY28E plus half of FY29E: the 12-month-forward earnings the market will look at in September 2027.

assumptions._note: GAM Research forecast drivers for BLS International (consolidated, Rs crore). Two reported segments on the company's EBITDA basis: Visa & Consular (incl. Citizenship Invest, iDATA, UK hotel and the new UIDAI Aadhaar Seva Kendras) and Digital Services (BLS E-Services group, incl. Atyati from 2-Jul-2026). Each segment's growth and margin come from a business-line build kept in `businessLines` and checked in tools/authoring/BLS.ctx.js. Screener's annual P&L moves bank charges (Rs29.9 cr in FY26) from costs to interest, so the 'unallocated' line adds them back to EBITDA (negative) and `interest` carries them. Net Profit is attributable to owners (BLS.patch.js: Screener 'Profit for EPS'); the tax line also carries minorities. Valued on P/E; the multiple is derived in BLS.ctx.js and written here by BLS.val.js.

visaCore._why: Visa & Consular ex-Aadhaar. FY26 +11.3%; Q1FY27 +21.6% reported, ~+15% excluding Aadhaar (Rs17.5 cr) and the UK hotel (Rs16 cr vs Rs2.5 cr): volumes flat at 11.3 lakh (West Asia war), net revenue per application +11%, Citizenship Invest Rs17.5 cr vs Rs11 cr. Management: 12-15% growth (travel 7-8% + ~5% pricing/mix), or 10-15% after expiries and wins (Aug-2026). +13% FY27E (Q1 at ~+15%), +11%, +10%. Margin 40.1% in FY26 and 40.3% in Q1FY27, guided 'maintain ~40%': 40.5% on the business ex-Aadhaar.

aadhaar._why: UIDAI work order Rs2,055 cr over six years (management: ~Rs2,500 cr of revenue over the term, i.e. ~Rs400-420 cr a year at full run-rate), plus Bihar enrolment centres (Rs100 cr). Rs17.5 cr in Q1FY27; phase 3 completes in Q2, full revenue 'from Q4 to Q1'. FY27E ~Rs180 cr (Q1 17.5, Q2 ~30, Q3 ~50, Q4 ~80), FY28E Rs400 cr, FY29E Rs420 cr. Margin: management said 15-20% (May-2026) and 10-15% (Aug-2026): we take 12.5%.

digitalOrganic._why: BLS E-Services ex-Atyati. FY26 +114% (Aadifidelis consolidated from Nov-2024); Q1FY27 +32% organically (both quarters include Aadifidelis): BC GTV +13%, loan distribution, Aadhaar-linked assisted services. +20%, +17%, +15%. Margin 7.0% in FY26, 8.0% in Q1FY27; management: margins rise with scale but stay structurally low (loan distribution earns 4-5%).

atyati._why: Bought 2-Jul-2026 for Rs156.82 cr: FY26 revenue ~Rs275 cr, EBITDA Rs20-21 cr (CFO, Aug-2026). FY27E = nine months (~Rs206 cr); ~+9-10% a year after. Margin 7.5% (Rs20.5 cr / Rs275 cr).

businessLines._check: visa = visaCore + aadhaar; digital = digitalOrganic + atyati. Segment growth/margin below are these sums (BLS.ctx.js throws if they differ by more than Rs1 cr).

segments.name: Visa & Consular Services
segments._why: Sum of the visa core and Aadhaar lines (businessLines). FY27E +22.8% (Q1 +21.6%), FY28E +19.9% (first full Aadhaar year), FY29E +9.3%.
segments._marginWhy: Mix: ~40.5% on visa and consular, 12.5% on Aadhaar, so the segment margin falls from 40.1% (FY26) to 38.3% (FY27E) and ~36.4-36.5% (FY28-29E).

segments.name: Digital Services
segments._why: Organic digital plus Atyati (businessLines): +37.8% in FY27E (+20% organic, ~18 points from Atyati), +20.7%, +14.2%.

assumptions._unallocLabel: Bank charges added back (Screener's annual P&L shows them in interest)
assumptions._unallocWhy: Company EBITDA = sum of segments (FY26: Rs737.8 + Rs81.0 = Rs818.8 cr vs Rs818.9 cr reported). Screener's annual EBITDA (Rs849 cr) excludes bank charges (Rs29.9 cr in FY26, 1.0% of revenue; AR note 26), which it puts in interest. We keep 1.0% of revenue and add the same amount to interest, so PBT is unaffected.
assumptions._capexWhy: Cash capex Rs137 cr in FY26, Rs161 cr in FY25. FY27E: remaining Aadhaar phases (Rs125 cr in all, Rs75 cr spent by Aug-2026), new visa centres and technology; Screener's gross block also takes new leased centres (right-of-use assets), which the engine adds only through capex, so the figures include ~Rs50-60 cr of new leases a year.
assumptions._depWhy: FY26 D&A Rs94 cr on an average gross block of ~Rs1,800 cr (which includes ~Rs1,213 cr of goodwill and intangibles; goodwill is not amortised). Q1FY27 Rs31.7 cr, 'a little higher' in Q2 as the Aadhaar centres complete: ~Rs140 cr in FY27E. 6.7% on gross block gives ~Rs141 cr.

otherTreasury._why: Items outside Screener's cash and investments: term deposits over 12 months Rs152.1 cr and accrued interest Rs16.9 cr (AR note 5) are treasury; the associate stake inside investments (Rs20.8 cr) is not; non-controlling interests at book (Rs320.2 cr, inside Screener's other liabilities) are counted as a claim like debt, so they come out of working capital (KIMS precedent). Lease liabilities (Rs200 cr) sit in Screener borrowings. Engine net treasury at Mar-26, after BLS.patch.js takes out the Atyati price (Rs156.8 cr) and the Rs45.2 cr spent on BLS E-Services shares, is ~Rs730 cr; the company's own net cash (before leases and minorities) was Rs1,434 cr (Rs1,617 cr at Jun-26).

assumptions._treasuryWhy: Applied to the engine's opening net treasury, which is net of leases and minority book value (~Rs520 cr that earn nothing), so the rate is higher than a deposit rate. Equivalent to ~5.0% on gross cash, deposits and debt funds: FY26 treasury income (deposits Rs52.1 cr, bonds Rs3.8 cr, fund gains Rs13.6 cr = Rs69.4 cr) was ~5.0% of average gross treasury (~Rs1,400 cr); Q1FY27 total other income Rs22.7 cr. FY27E ~Rs73 cr on ~Rs1,463 cr gross after the Atyati and BLS E-Services payments; the rate steps down as the base grows (no acquisitions or buyback assumed).
assumptions._otherIncomeWhy: Non-treasury other income (AR note 23): insurance and commission Rs7.2 cr, miscellaneous Rs10.1 cr, other interest Rs0.7 cr = Rs18.0 cr in FY26. The FX gain (Rs7.9 cr, mostly one-off) is not forecast. FY27E total ~Rs91 cr vs Rs95.2 cr in FY26 and Rs22.7 cr x 4 = Rs91 cr in Q1FY27.
assumptions._interestLabel: Finance cost (leases, borrowings) plus bank charges (Screener basis)
assumptions._interestWhy: Finance cost Rs23.2 cr in FY26 and Rs7.7 cr in Q1FY27 (new Aadhaar leases): Rs33 cr, Rs36 cr, Rs38 cr; plus bank charges at 1.0% of revenue (see unallocated).
assumptions._taxWhy: Tax PLUS minorities (engine workaround; Net Profit is attributable). FY26: PBT Rs797 cr, tax Rs73 cr (9.2%), minorities Rs37 cr, owners' profit Rs687 cr = 13.8% leakage. Q1FY27: PBT Rs236 cr, tax Rs34 cr (14.4%), minorities Rs12 cr = 19.5%. Management guides ~12% tax for FY27 (UAE free zone; India's share rising with Aadhaar); a UAE rate change could add ~1 point. Minorities ~5.5% of PBT: ~47% of BLS E-Services (BLS 53.2% after Apr-Aug 2026 purchases), 43% of Aadifidelis, 9% of Zero Mass, with Atyati inside BLS E-Services. 12% + 5.5% = 17.5% FY27E; 18% after.
assumptions._payoutWhy: FY26 DPS Rs2.50 (Rs103 cr, 15% of owners' profit); FY25 ~8%. Management prefers M&A to buybacks; 15% kept.

dcf._betaWhy: Tender-driven revenue from a few governments, regulatory events (MEA debarment and its reversal), FX and a promoter-controlled board: 1.0 (Ke 12.5%) despite net cash.
dcf._tgWhy: Cross-border travel and outsourced visa volumes grow ~7-9% a year (industry estimates in the company deck); 6% in perpetuity.
dcf._fadeGrowthWhy: Revenue growth fades from ~11% (FY29E) to 8% over 15 years.
dcf._fadeMarginWhy: EBITDA margin drifts from ~24.7% (FY29E, Screener basis) to 24% as Digital (8%) and Aadhaar keep growing faster than visa.
dcf._fadeCapexWhy: Asset-light (leased centres): capex and depreciation ~3% of revenue.
dcf._minorityNote: The DCF counts minorities only at book (Rs320 cr inside otherTreasury); their share of BLS E-Services' market value is higher, so the DCF overstates value per share slightly.

bull.label: Bull
bull.narrative: Visa volumes recover after the West Asia war and new global contracts (Slovakia, Cyprus, a further European tender) ramp; Aadhaar runs at the top of its margin range; digital keeps compounding.

bear.label: Bear
bear.narrative: A large European contract is lost or re-tendered at lower prices, visa volumes stay flat, Indian-mission work shrinks (the MEA issues a fresh notice), and Aadhaar earns the bottom of its range.

methods.name: P/E
methods.why: How the street values BLS: P/E on forward EPS (IDBI Capital, the only active broker: 21.5x FY27E at its Dec-2025 initiation; May-2026 note's year and multiple behind a login). Multiple = own one-year-forward P/E median since Apr-2021 x the sector move of TBO Tek's widened travel + internet set (IRCTC, Thomas Cook, Info Edge, IndiaMART) vs five-year medians; derived in BLS.ctx.js and written by BLS.val.js.

methods.name: EV/EBITDA
methods.why: Values the operating business and the treasury separately (own forward EV/EBITDA history computed in BLS.ctx.js).

methods.name: DCF
methods.why: Tests whether cash flows support the price: 15-year FCFF, Ke 12.5%, terminal growth 6%, plus net treasury (after leases and minorities at book).
